angular momentum quantum number, l: The quantum number that sets an orbital's shape, ranging from 0 to n-1, where 0, 1, 2, 3 give s, p, d, f orbitals.
anion: A negatively charged ion formed when an atom gains one or more electrons, making it larger than the parent atom.
anomalous electron configuration: An electron configuration departing from the normal filling order for the extra stability of half-filled or full d subshells.
atomic mass: The weighted average mass of all naturally occurring isotopes of an element.
atomic mass unit: A standard unit of atomic and molecular mass defined as exactly one-twelfth the mass of a carbon-12 atom.
atomic number: The number of protons in an atom's nucleus, which defines the identity of the element.
atomic radius: The distance from the nucleus to the outermost electrons, decreasing across a period and increasing down a group.
aufbau principle: The rule that electrons fill orbitals from lowest to highest energy as atoms seek their lowest-energy arrangement.
avogadro's number: The constant 6.022 x 10^23, the number of particles in one mole.
base peak: The most intense peak in a mass spectrum, assigned a relative abundance of 100 percent.
binding energy: The minimum energy needed to remove an electron from an atomic subshell, measured in MJ/mol.
boiling point: The temperature at which a liquid's vapor pressure equals atmospheric pressure.
bond polarity: The unequal distribution of electron density in a covalent bond caused by an electronegativity difference between atoms.
cation: A positively charged ion formed when an atom loses one or more electrons, making it smaller than the parent atom.
chromatography: A separation technique exploiting different distribution of components between a stationary and a mobile phase.
colloid: A heterogeneous mixture with particles 1 to 1000 nanometers dispersed in a medium, small enough to stay suspended.
combustion analysis: An experimental method finding a compound's composition by fully burning a sample and measuring the CO2 and H2O produced.
compound: A pure substance of two or more elements chemically bonded in a fixed ratio.
core electrons: Inner-shell electrons that do not participate in bonding, held tightly with high binding energy.
coulomb's law: The principle that electrostatic force is proportional to the product of charges and inversely proportional to distance squared.
covalent radius: Half the distance between the nuclei of two identical atoms joined by a single covalent bond.
d block: The region of transition metals where electrons fill the (n-1)d orbitals.
de broglie wavelength: The wavelength associated with a moving particle, equal to Planck's constant divided by its momentum.
degenerate orbitals: Orbitals that have equal energy, such as the three 2p orbitals within an atom.
dimensional analysis: A problem-solving method arranging conversion factors so unwanted units cancel.
distillation: A separation technique using differences in boiling point to vaporize and then condense components.
effective nuclear charge: The net positive charge a valence electron feels after accounting for shielding by inner electrons.
effective nuclear charge trend: The tendency for effective nuclear charge to rise across a period as nuclear charge outpaces shielding.
effective nuclear charge, z-eff: The net positive charge an electron actually feels after inner-electron shielding, roughly nuclear charge minus shielding electrons.
effective nuclear charge, zeff: The net positive charge a valence electron feels, nuclear charge minus shielding, setting how tightly it is held.
electron configuration: A notation describing the distribution of electrons among orbitals using subshell symbols and superscripts.
electron-electron repulsion: The Coulombic repulsion between electrons sharing an orbital or nearby space, raising the system's energy.
electronegativity: An atom's tendency to attract shared electrons in a covalent bond.
electrostatic attraction: The force pulling oppositely charged particles together, such as protons and electrons.
element: A pure substance of atoms with the same atomic number that cannot be broken into simpler substances chemically.
empirical formula: A formula giving the simplest whole-number ratio of atoms in a compound.
exchange energy: The quantum stabilization gained when parallel-spin electrons occupy different orbitals of the same subshell.
f block: The region of lanthanides and actinides where electrons fill the (n-2)f orbitals.
filtration: A separation technique passing a mixture through a porous barrier to separate particles by size.
first ionization energy: The energy needed to remove the most loosely held electron from a neutral gaseous atom.
first ionization energy, ie1: The energy needed to remove one electron from a ground-state neutral gaseous atom to form a +1 cation.
formula mass: The sum of the atomic masses of all atoms in a chemical formula.
fractional abundance: The proportion of a particular isotope expressed as a decimal between 0 and 1.
fractional distillation: A distillation using a fractionating column to provide repeated vaporization-condensation cycles for close boiling points.
fragmentation: The breaking of bonds during ionization, producing smaller charged pieces from a parent molecule.
half-filled subshell stability: The extra stability seen when each orbital of a subshell holds exactly one electron, maximizing exchange energy.
heisenberg uncertainty principle: The limit that the product of uncertainties in position and momentum cannot be smaller than h/4 pi.
heterogeneous mixture: A mixture of nonuniform composition with visibly or microscopically distinct regions.
homogeneous mixture: A mixture uniform at the particle level, also called a solution.
hund's rule: The principle that electrons singly occupy each orbital of a subshell before pairing, to minimize repulsion.
intermolecular forces: Attractions between molecules, including dispersion, dipole-dipole, hydrogen bonding, and ion-dipole forces.
ionic radius: The effective radius of an ion in a crystal; cations are smaller and anions larger than their parent atoms.
ionization: The process of removing or adding electrons to make a charged particle.
ionization energy: The energy needed to remove the outermost electron from a gaseous atom.
isoelectronic series: A set of ions and atoms with the same electron configuration but different nuclear charges.
isoelectronic species: Atoms or ions with identical electron configurations, where size depends only on nuclear charge.
isotope: Atoms of the same element with equal protons but different neutron numbers and therefore different nuclear masses.
isotope pattern: The characteristic peak-intensity distribution arising from the natural abundances of an element's isotopes.
magnetic quantum number, ml: The quantum number specifying an orbital's spatial orientation, ranging from -l to +l.
mass number: The total number of protons and neutrons in an atom's nucleus, always a whole number.
mass spectrometer: An instrument that ionizes a sample, separates ions by mass-to-charge ratio, and measures their abundances.
mass-to-charge ratio: The quantity m/z measured by a mass spectrometer, an ion's mass divided by its charge.
mechanistic reasoning: An explanation including the causal chain linking observations to underlying principles.
mixture: Two or more substances combined while keeping their own chemical identities, held by intermolecular forces.
mobile phase: The phase in chromatography that carries components through or over the stationary phase.
molar mass: The mass in grams of one mole of a substance, numerically equal to its formula mass in amu.
mole: The SI unit of amount of substance, defined as exactly 6.02214076 x 10^23 representative particles.
molecular formula: A formula giving the actual number of atoms of each element in a molecule.
molecular ion peak: The mass spectrum peak for the intact molecule with a single electron removed.
node: A region where the wavefunction is zero and the probability of finding an electron is zero.
nuclear charge: The total positive charge of the nucleus, equal to the number of protons.
nucleon: A particle of the atomic nucleus, either a proton or a neutron.
orbital: A three-dimensional probability distribution describing where an electron is likely found.
p block: The groups 13 to 18 region where valence electrons enter p orbitals.
parent ion: Another name for the molecular ion, the original molecule with one electron removed before fragmentation.
partial charge: A fractional charge (delta+ or delta-) on an atom from unequal electron sharing in a polar bond.
partitioning: The distribution of a solute between two phases based on relative solubility or intermolecular affinity.
pauli exclusion principle: The principle that no two electrons in an atom can have all four quantum numbers identical.
pauling scale: The most common electronegativity scale, based on bond dissociation energies, with fluorine set at 4.0.
peak height: The vertical size of a PES peak, proportional to the number of electrons in that subshell.
peak position: The location of a peak on a PES x-axis, indicating the binding energy of that subshell's electrons.
penetration: The greater probability of an s electron being found near the nucleus than p, d, or f electrons of the same shell.
percent composition: The mass percentage of each element in a compound.
period trend: The decrease in atomic radius moving left to right across a period due to rising nuclear charge.
phase: A region of matter uniform in composition and properties, bounded by a surface where properties change abruptly.
photoelectron spectroscopy, pes: A technique measuring electron binding energies by ejecting electrons with high-energy photons and measuring their kinetic energy.
polar covalent bond: A covalent bond with unequal electron sharing from an electronegativity difference, giving partial charges.
principal energy level: The main energy shell an electron occupies, labeled by quantum number n.
principal quantum number, n: A positive integer setting the energy level and average distance from the nucleus.
probability density: The square of the wavefunction at a point, the probability per unit volume of finding an electron there.
proton to electron ratio: The relationship of nuclear charge to electron number, setting the net attraction each electron feels.
pure substance: Matter made of only one kind of particle, a single element's atoms or a single compound's molecules.
quantization: The restriction of a physical quantity to discrete rather than continuous values.
relative abundance: The proportion of a given ion detected relative to the most abundant ion in a spectrum.
relative number of electrons: The quantity shown by PES peak height, indicating how many electrons occupy a subshell.
representative particle: The smallest unit retaining a substance's chemical identity, such as an atom, molecule, or formula unit.
retention: The slowing of a component in chromatography due to attraction to the stationary phase.
rf value: The retention factor, a component's distance traveled divided by the solvent front's distance.
s block: The groups 1 and 2 region where valence electrons enter s orbitals.
shell collapse: The disappearance of an entire principal energy level when a cation forms, causing a sharp drop in radius.
shielding: The reduction in effective nuclear charge an outer electron feels due to repulsion from inner electrons.
shielding effect: The reduced nuclear attraction on outer electrons caused by repulsion from inner electrons.
shielding/screening: The decrease in nuclear attraction on valence electrons caused by repulsion from inner shells.
solution: A homogeneous mixture of a solute dissolved in a solvent, uniform at the molecular level.
spin quantum number, ms: The quantum number describing an electron's intrinsic spin, either +1/2 or -1/2.
standing wave: A fixed wave pattern formed when a wave constructively interferes with itself.
stationary phase: The fixed phase in chromatography that retards components attracted to it.
stoichiometry: The quantitative study of reactants and products using mole ratios from balanced equations.
successive ionization energies: The sequence of energies for removing electrons one by one, with large jumps marking shell changes.
suspension: A heterogeneous mixture of visible particles that settle out over time under gravity.
transition metal cation: A cation formed when a transition metal loses electrons, with 4s electrons removed before 3d.
valence electrons: The outermost electrons of an atom that participate in chemical bonding.
valence subshell: The outermost occupied subshell, holding the lowest-binding-energy, most easily removed electrons.
vapor pressure: The pressure exerted by vapor in equilibrium with its liquid; higher when intermolecular forces are weak.
wave-particle duality: The principle that all matter exhibits both wave and particle properties.
weighted average: An average where each value is multiplied by a weight reflecting its frequency before summing.
whole-number multiplier: The integer multiplying an empirical formula's subscripts to give the molecular formula.
allotrope: A different structural form of the same element in the same physical state, like diamond and graphite.
alloy: A mixture of a metal with one or more other elements that alters the host metal's properties.
axial position: In a trigonal bipyramid, the two positions 180 degrees apart along the axis, each with three 90-degree neighbors.
bent geometry: A molecular geometry with two bonded atoms and one or two lone pairs giving a V-shaped arrangement.
binary acid: An acid containing hydrogen and only one other element, named with hydro- prefix and -ic acid suffix.
binary covalent compound: A covalent compound of exactly two nonmetal elements, named with Greek prefixes.
binding energy comparison: The analysis of relative binding energies between elements to verify identity or explain spectral differences.
bond dipole: A vector representing charge separation in a polar bond, pointing from the partial positive to partial negative end.
bond energy: The enthalpy needed to break one mole of a specific bond in the gas phase, rising with bond order.
bond length: The equilibrium distance between two bonded nuclei, decreasing as bond order increases.
bond order: The number of bonding electron pairs between two atoms.
bonding electrons: Valence electrons occupying bonding molecular orbitals that directly form chemical bonds.
brittleness: The tendency of a material to shatter rather than deform under stress, characteristic of ionic compounds.
charge balance: The principle that an ionic compound must be electrically neutral overall.
charge density: The ratio of an ion's charge to its volume, affecting the strength of metallic bonding.
covalent compound: A compound formed by electron sharing between nonmetal atoms.
d orbital participation: The involvement of d orbitals in bonding, allowing elements in period 3 and beyond to exceed an octet.
decision tree: A sequence of binary choices guiding compound classification and naming.
delocalized electrons: Electrons spread over several atoms rather than tied to one bond, enabling conductivity in metals and graphite.
delocalized pi system: A network of overlapping p orbitals across several atoms, spreading pi electron density over the whole system.
dipole cancellation: The summing of equal, opposite bond dipoles to zero, producing a nonpolar molecule despite polar bonds.
dipole-dipole force: An intermolecular attraction between polar molecules, aligning partial positive and partial negative regions.
ductility: The ability of a material to be drawn into wire, arising from the metallic electron sea.
electrical conductivity: The ability of a substance to carry current, requiring mobile charged particles.
electron delocalization: The spreading of electron density over several atoms rather than between two, as in resonance-stabilized molecules.
electron density redistribution: The shift in electron probability distribution when atoms form chemical bonds.
electron domain: A region of electron density around a central atom, counting bonds and lone pairs.
electron domain geometry: The three-dimensional arrangement of all electron domains around a central atom.
electron geometry: The 3D arrangement of all electron domains, both bonding pairs and lone pairs, around a central atom.
electron sea model: A model in which metal atoms contribute valence electrons to a delocalized cloud surrounding cation lattices.
electron shielding effect: The reduction of nuclear attraction on outer electrons by inner electrons, increasing down a group.
electronegativity difference: The absolute difference in electronegativity between two bonded atoms, setting bond polarity.
electronegativity placement rule: The rule that negative formal charge should sit on the more electronegative atom.
equatorial position: In a trigonal bipyramid, the three positions 120 degrees apart in the central plane, preferred by lone pairs.
equivalent resonance contributors: Resonance structures of identical energy and formal charge distribution that contribute equally to the hybrid.
expanded octet: A bonding arrangement where an atom holds more than eight valence electrons, possible in period 3 and beyond.
formal charge: The hypothetical charge an atom would have if bonding electrons were shared equally, FC = V - N - (B/2).
formal charge minimization: The principle that the best Lewis structure keeps all formal charges as close to zero as possible.
greek prefixes: Numerical prefixes in covalent naming such as mono, di, tri, tetra, and penta.
head-on overlap: Orbital overlap end-to-end along the internuclear axis, forming a cylindrically symmetric sigma bond.
homolytic cleavage: Bond breaking where each atom takes one electron, producing two radicals and defining bond dissociation energy.
hybridization: The mixing of atomic orbitals into equivalent hybrid orbitals that explain molecular geometry and bonding.
hydration: The process where water molecules surround and stabilize dissolved ions by ion-dipole attraction.
hydrogen bonding: A strong dipole-dipole attraction when H bonded to N, O, or F interacts with a lone pair on another N, O, or F.
intermolecular force: An attraction between separate molecules, including dispersion, dipole-dipole, and hydrogen bonding.
interstitial alloy: An alloy where small foreign atoms occupy the gaps between host metal atoms, as in steel.
intramolecular force: An attraction holding atoms together within a molecule, specifically a covalent bond.
ionic compound: A compound held by electrostatic attraction between cations and anions in a crystal lattice.
ionic lattice: A 3D crystal structure of cations and anions arranged in a repeating pattern.
lattice distortion: Irregularity in a metal lattice from differently sized foreign atoms, hindering layer slip and increasing hardness.
lattice energy: The energy needed to separate one mole of an ionic solid into infinitely distant gaseous ions.
like dissolves like: The solubility principle that polar solvents dissolve polar solutes and nonpolar dissolve nonpolar.
london dispersion force: A weak intermolecular force from instantaneous dipoles caused by momentary electron fluctuations.
lone pair: A valence electron pair not shared in a covalent bond, occupying space and affecting molecular shape.
lone pair repulsion: The electrostatic repulsion from lone pairs, stronger than bonding-pair repulsion because lone pairs spread out more.
main group metal: A metal of groups 1, 2, or 13 forming ions of predictable charge, needing no Stock notation.
malleability: The ability of a material to be hammered into thin sheets, arising from the metallic electron sea.
metallic bond: The electrostatic attraction between metal cations and a surrounding sea of delocalized electrons.
metallic character: An atom's tendency to release valence electrons, increasing down a group and decreasing across a period.
molecular geometry: The 3D arrangement of only the atoms around a central atom, excluding lone pairs from the name.
net dipole moment: The vector sum of all bond dipoles in a molecule; nonzero means polar, zero means nonpolar.
network covalent solid: A solid where atoms are connected by continuous covalent bonds throughout the crystal.
non-directional bonding: The feature of metallic bonding where attraction is not aimed between specific atoms.
nonpolar covalent bond: A covalent bond with equal electron sharing between atoms of equal or very similar electronegativity.
nonpolar molecule: A molecule with zero net dipole moment, either from nonpolar bonds or symmetric cancellation of polar bonds.
oxidation state: The effective charge an atom has in a compound after assigning bonding electrons to the more electronegative atom.
oxyacid: An acid containing hydrogen, oxygen, and another element, named from its parent oxyanion.
oxyanion: A polyatomic anion with a central atom bonded to one or more oxygen atoms, named with -ate or -ite.
peak shift: The change in a PES peak's binding-energy position when an atom is in a different chemical environment.
period 2 limitation: The strict rule that C, N, O, and F can never exceed eight valence electrons, lacking accessible d orbitals.
periodic trend: A systematic variation in element properties following the structure of the periodic table.
photoelectric effect: The ejection of electrons when photon energy exceeds their binding energy, with excess becoming kinetic energy.
pi bond: A covalent bond from side-by-side overlap of parallel p orbitals, with density above and below the bond axis.
planarity: The geometric condition where all atoms of a group lie in a single plane, often from sp2 hybridization.
polar molecule: A molecule with a nonzero net dipole moment from an asymmetric arrangement of polar bonds.
polyatomic ion: A charged particle of two or more covalently bonded atoms acting as a single unit in ionic bonding.
prefix elision: Dropping the final vowel of a Greek prefix before a vowel, as tetra plus oxide becomes tetroxide.
relative peak height: The proportional height of a PES peak, indicating the number of electrons in that subshell.
repulsion hierarchy: The VSEPR ranking that lone pair-lone pair repulsion exceeds lone pair-bond pair, which exceeds bond pair-bond pair.
resonance hybrid: The true structure of a molecule as a weighted blend of its resonance contributors.
resonance structures: Multiple valid Lewis structures differing only in electron placement, none alone fully describing the molecule.
restricted rotation: The blocking of rotation around a bond by a pi bond, which would require breaking the p-orbital overlap.
seesaw geometry: A molecular geometry with four bonded atoms and one lone pair derived from trigonal bipyramidal electron geometry.
side-by-side overlap: Parallel overlap of p orbitals forming a pi bond with density off the internuclear axis.
sigma bond: A covalent bond from head-on orbital overlap with electron density along the internuclear axis.
sigma framework: The network of sigma bonds forming the skeletal connectivity of a molecule.
sp hybridization: The mixing of one s and one p orbital giving two linear hybrids 180 degrees apart.
sp2 hybridization: The mixing of one s and two p orbitals giving three trigonal planar hybrids 120 degrees apart.
sp3 hybridization: The mixing of one s and three p orbitals giving four tetrahedral hybrids about 109.5 degrees apart.
spectroscopic evidence: Data from spectroscopy used to determine or confirm molecular structure and composition.
stock notation: Roman numerals indicating the charge of a metal cation that can have multiple oxidation states.
sublimation: The direct transition of a substance from solid to gas without passing through the liquid phase.
subshell: A subdivision of a principal energy level designated s, p, d, or f, made of orbitals of equal energy.
substitutional alloy: An alloy where foreign atoms replace host metal atoms in the lattice.
systematic name: A name assigned by formal nomenclature rules rather than a common name.
systematic structure analysis: A step-by-step procedure for deducing molecular structure from given data.
tetrahedral electron geometry: An electron geometry with four electron domains arranged about 109.5 degrees apart.
tetrahedral geometry: A molecular geometry with four bonded atoms at the corners of a tetrahedron.
total electron count: The sum of all valence electrons accounted for in constructing a Lewis structure.
transition metal: A d-block element capable of forming ions with multiple charges and colored compounds.
trigonal pyramidal: A molecular geometry with three bonded atoms and one lone pair on the central atom.
vector: A quantity with both magnitude and direction, used to represent bond dipoles.
vector addition: The combining of vectors accounting for direction, used to find a net dipole moment.
vsepr theory: Valence shell electron pair repulsion theory, predicting molecular shape from electron-domain repulsion.
activity coefficient: A factor correcting concentration for nonideal behavior of ions in solution.
alpha helix: A coiled secondary-structure motif of proteins stabilized by hydrogen bonds along the backbone.
anomalous phase behavior: Unexpected phase behavior such as water expanding on freezing rather than contracting.
anomalous property: A property deviating from expected trends, like water's high boiling point from hydrogen bonding.
base pairing: Hydrogen bonding between complementary nucleotide bases holding the DNA double helix together.
beta sheet: A secondary-structure motif of proteins formed by hydrogen bonds between extended strands.
body-centered cubic, bcc: A unit cell with atoms at each corner and one in the center of the cube.
boiling: The rapid vaporization throughout a liquid when its vapor pressure equals the external pressure.
boiling point elevation constant, kb: A solvent-specific constant relating molality to the rise in boiling point.
boundary line: A line on a phase diagram marking conditions where two phases coexist in equilibrium.
carbonyl absorption: A strong infrared absorption near 1700 cm-1 indicating a C=O group.
categorical imf trap: The error of ranking intermolecular forces by category alone without considering cumulative strength.
chemical equivalence: The condition where atoms in identical environments give a single NMR signal.
chemical shift: The position of an NMR signal relative to a reference, reflecting an atom's electronic environment.
clausius-clapeyron equation: An equation relating vapor pressure to temperature and the enthalpy of vaporization.
colligative property: A solution property depending on the number of solute particles, not their identity.
coordination number: The number of nearest neighbors surrounding an atom or ion in a structure.
crenation: The shriveling of a cell placed in a hypertonic solution as water leaves it.
critical point: The temperature and pressure beyond which liquid and gas phases become indistinguishable.
critical temperature: The temperature above which a gas cannot be liquefied by pressure alone.
cumulative imf model: A model evaluating total intermolecular attraction by adding all contributing forces.
decision framework: A structured set of criteria guiding a sequence of analytical choices.
decompression sickness: A condition from dissolved gases forming bubbles when pressure drops too quickly, explained by Henry's law.
degree of dissociation, α: The fraction of dissolved electrolyte that separates into ions.
degree of unsaturation: The number of rings and pi bonds in a molecule, calculated from its molecular formula.
delocalized pi electrons: Pi electrons spread over several atoms rather than confined between two.
denaturation: The loss of a protein's functional structure when intermolecular forces holding its shape are disrupted.
density inversion: The unusual case where a solid is less dense than its liquid, as with ice floating on water.
deshielding: A downfield NMR shift caused by reduced electron density around a nucleus.
dipole-dipole forces: Attractions between polar molecules aligning their partial charges.
dipole-dipole interaction: The attraction between the partial charges of neighboring polar molecules.
effective van't hoff factor: The actual number of dissolved particles per formula unit, reduced by ion pairing.
electron cloud: The region of probable electron location around a nucleus.
electronegativity threshold: An electronegativity-difference cutoff used to classify a bond as ionic, polar, or nonpolar.
endothermic dissolution: A dissolving process that absorbs heat, cooling the surroundings.
enthalpy of hydration: The energy released when gaseous ions are surrounded and stabilized by water molecules.
enthalpy of solution: The total enthalpy change when a solute dissolves in a solvent.
enthalpy of vaporization: The energy needed to convert one mole of liquid to gas at constant temperature.
entropy of mixing: The increase in disorder when substances combine to form a solution.
entropy-driven dissolution: A dissolving process favored by increased entropy despite an unfavorable enthalpy.
face-centered cubic, fcc: A unit cell with atoms at each corner and the center of each face.
fingerprint region: The complex lower-wavenumber region of an IR spectrum unique to each molecule.
fragmentation pattern: The characteristic set of fragment peaks in a mass spectrum used to identify a molecule.
freezing point depression constant, kf: A solvent-specific constant relating molality to the drop in freezing point.
functional group region: The higher-wavenumber IR region where characteristic functional-group absorptions appear.
gibbs free energy: A thermodynamic quantity combining enthalpy and entropy to predict spontaneity, G = H - TS.
hardness: A material's resistance to scratching or deformation.
henry's law: The principle that a gas's solubility is proportional to its partial pressure above the liquid.
henry's law constant: The proportionality constant relating a gas's partial pressure to its solubility.
hexagonal lattice: A crystal lattice based on a hexagonal arrangement of atoms.
homologous series: A family of compounds differing by a repeating unit, such as successive CH2 groups.
hydrogen bond acceptor: An atom with a lone pair, such as N, O, or F, that accepts a hydrogen bond.
hydrogen bond acceptor capacity: The number of lone pairs a molecule has available to accept hydrogen bonds.
hydrogen bond donor: A hydrogen bonded to N, O, or F that can participate in a hydrogen bond.
hydrogen bond donor capacity: The number of N-H, O-H, or F-H groups a molecule has available to donate hydrogen bonds.
hydrogen bond network: An interconnected system of hydrogen bonds linking many molecules.
hydrogen bonding network: A three-dimensional web of hydrogen bonds, as in liquid water or ice.
hydrophobic effect: The tendency of nonpolar groups to cluster in water, driven by the water's entropy.
hypertonic solution: A solution with higher solute concentration than a cell, drawing water out of the cell.
hypotonic solution: A solution with lower solute concentration than a cell, driving water into the cell.
induced dipole: A temporary dipole created when a nearby charge or dipole distorts an electron cloud.
instantaneous dipole: A momentary dipole from random electron fluctuation, the origin of dispersion forces.
integration: In NMR, the relative area under a signal, proportional to the number of equivalent atoms.
interlayer forces: Weak forces between layers of a layered solid like graphite.
intermolecular network: An extended structure of intermolecular forces linking many molecules.
intralayer bonding: The strong covalent bonding within a single layer of a layered solid.
ion pairing: The association of oppositely charged ions in solution, reducing the effective particle count.
ion-dipole interaction: The attraction between an ion and the partial charge of a polar molecule.
ionic solid: A solid of cations and anions held in a lattice by electrostatic attraction.
isomers: Compounds with the same molecular formula but different arrangements of atoms.
isotonic solution: A solution with the same solute concentration as a cell, producing no net water movement.
london dispersion forces: Weak attractions from temporary dipoles present in all molecules.
lubricant: A substance that reduces friction, such as graphite whose layers slide easily.
m/z ratio: The mass-to-charge ratio measured in mass spectrometry.
maximum density temperature: The temperature at which a liquid reaches its greatest density, about 4 degrees Celsius for water.
melting point: The temperature at which a solid changes to a liquid.
melting temperature: The temperature at which a solid's structure breaks down into the liquid phase.
metallic solid: A solid of metal atoms held by metallic bonding with a delocalized electron sea.
miscibility: The ability of two liquids to mix in all proportions.
molality, m: The number of moles of solute per kilogram of solvent.
molar mass correlation: The trend that larger molar mass increases dispersion forces and thus boiling point.
molecular ion, m⁺: The intact molecule with one electron removed, giving a peak at the molecular mass.
molecular solid: A solid of discrete molecules held together by intermolecular forces.
net imf strength: The overall strength of all intermolecular forces acting on a molecule.
nonvolatile solute: A solute with negligible vapor pressure that lowers a solvent's vapor pressure.
normal boiling point: The boiling temperature at exactly 1 atmosphere of pressure.
osmotic pressure, π: The pressure needed to stop osmosis across a semipermeable membrane.
packing efficiency: The fraction of a unit cell's volume occupied by its atoms.
partial positive charge: A delta-plus region on an atom from unequal electron sharing in a polar bond.
partial pressure: The pressure one gas in a mixture would exert if it alone occupied the volume.
phase diagram: A graph of pressure versus temperature showing the stable phase under each condition.
phase stability: The range of conditions under which a particular phase is the most stable.
polarizability: The ease with which an atom's or molecule's electron cloud is distorted, increasing dispersion forces.
pressure melting: The lowering of a substance's melting point under increased pressure, as with ice.
raoult's law: The principle that a solution's vapor pressure equals the solvent mole fraction times its pure vapor pressure.
semipermeable membrane: A barrier allowing solvent but not solute to pass, enabling osmosis.
simple cubic, sc: A unit cell with atoms only at the eight corners of a cube.
size advantage: An effect where larger atoms with greater polarizability have stronger dispersion forces.
spontaneous process: A process that occurs without continuous external input, having negative Gibbs free energy.
strong electrolyte: A solute that fully dissociates into ions in solution.
supercritical fluid: A substance above its critical point with properties of both liquid and gas.
surface area: The exposed outer area of a substance, increasing contact for dispersion forces.
surface area effect: The trend that greater molecular surface area increases dispersion forces and boiling point.
surface tension: The energy needed to expand a liquid's surface, arising from cohesive intermolecular forces.
systematic elimination: A method ruling out possibilities one by one to reach a conclusion.
thermodynamic equilibrium: A state where a system's properties are unchanging and no net process occurs.
total intermolecular force: The combined effect of all intermolecular attractions acting on a molecule.
triangulation: Determining an unknown by combining several independent lines of evidence.
triple point: The unique temperature and pressure where solid, liquid, and gas coexist in equilibrium.
unit cell: The smallest repeating unit of a crystal lattice.
valence shell distance: The distance of the valence shell from the nucleus, affecting bonding and reactivity.
van't hoff factor, i: The number of particles a formula unit produces in solution.
vapor pressure lowering: The decrease in a solvent's vapor pressure when a nonvolatile solute is added.
viscosity: A liquid's resistance to flow, increasing with stronger intermolecular forces.
volatility: The tendency of a substance to vaporize, higher when intermolecular forces are weak.
wavenumber: The reciprocal of wavelength used as the x-axis unit in infrared spectroscopy.
acidic solution method: A method for balancing redox half-reactions by adding H+ and water in acidic conditions.
activity series: A ranking of metals by reactivity, predicting which displaces another from solution.
actual yield: The measured amount of product obtained from a reaction.
analyte: The substance being measured or determined in an analysis.
anode: The electrode where oxidation occurs in an electrochemical cell.
balanced chemical equation: An equation with equal numbers of each atom on both sides, obeying conservation of mass.
balanced equation: A chemical equation with coefficients making atoms equal on both sides.
basic solution method: A method for balancing redox half-reactions by adding OH- and water in basic conditions.
bronsted-lowry acid: A species that donates a proton in a chemical reaction.
bronsted-lowry base: A species that accepts a proton in a chemical reaction.
buffer capacity: The amount of acid or base a buffer can neutralize before its pH changes significantly.
buffer region: The flat portion of a titration curve where a buffer resists pH change.
burette: A graduated glass tube used to deliver precise volumes during titration.
cathode: The electrode where reduction occurs in an electrochemical cell.
coefficient: The number placed before a formula in an equation to balance atoms.
collection over water: A gas-collection method displacing water, requiring correction for water vapor pressure.
combustion reaction: A reaction of a substance with oxygen releasing heat and forming oxides.
common ion effect: The reduced solubility or ionization of a substance when a shared ion is already present.
complete ionic equation: An equation showing all soluble ionic species as separate ions.
concentration cell: A galvanic cell generating voltage from a difference in ion concentration.
conditional reasoning: Logical analysis based on whether specific conditions are met.
conjugate acid of a weak base: The species formed when a weak base gains a proton.
conjugate acid-base pair: Two species differing by a single proton.
conjugate base of a weak acid: The species formed when a weak acid loses a proton.
coupled reaction: Pairing a nonspontaneous reaction with a spontaneous one to drive it forward.
dalton's law of partial pressures: The principle that total pressure equals the sum of the partial pressures of all gases.
decomposition reaction: A reaction where one compound breaks into two or more simpler substances.
derived constant: A constant obtained by combining other known constants.
diluent: The solvent added to reduce the concentration of a solution.
dilution: The process of lowering concentration by adding more solvent.
displacement reaction: A reaction where one element replaces another in a compound.
double displacement reaction: A reaction where two compounds exchange ions to form two new compounds.
driving force: The factor, such as gas, precipitate, or water formation, that pushes a reaction forward.
electrolytic cell: A cell using electrical energy to drive a nonspontaneous redox reaction.
electron cancellation: Balancing electrons gained and lost when combining redox half-reactions.
electron pair acceptor: A Lewis acid that accepts a lone pair to form a bond.
electroplating: Depositing a metal layer onto a surface using electrolysis.
endpoint: The point in a titration where the indicator changes color.
equilibrium in electrochemistry: The state where a cell reaches zero potential and reaction quotient equals the equilibrium constant.
equilibrium limitation: The constraint that a reaction proceeds only until equilibrium is reached.
equilibrium position: The relative amounts of reactants and products present at equilibrium.
equivalence point: The titration point where moles of acid and base are stoichiometrically equal.
excess reactant: The reactant remaining after the limiting reactant is fully consumed.
excess reagent: The reagent present in more than the stoichiometrically required amount.
excess reagent remaining: The amount of excess reagent left after a reaction completes.
external circuit: The wire path through which electrons flow between electrodes in a cell.
faraday constant: The charge of one mole of electrons, about 96485 coulombs per mole.
faraday law of electrolysis: The law relating the amount of substance produced at an electrode to the charge passed.
full ionic equation: An equation showing all dissolved strong electrolytes as separate ions.
galvanic cell: An electrochemical cell that generates electricity from a spontaneous redox reaction.
gas constant r: The proportionality constant in the ideal gas law, 0.0821 L atm per mol K.
half-equivalence point: The titration point where half the acid is neutralized and pH equals pKa.
half-reaction: One half of a redox reaction showing either oxidation or reduction.
henderson-hasselbalch equation: An equation giving buffer pH from pKa and the ratio of conjugate base to acid.
hydrolysis: A reaction in which water splits a bond, often changing the pH of a salt solution.
ice table: A table tracking Initial, Change, and Equilibrium concentrations in an equilibrium problem.
ideal gas law: The relationship PV = nRT describing the behavior of an ideal gas.
indicator: A substance that changes color to signal the endpoint of a titration.
ion product, q: The reaction quotient for a dissolving ionic compound, compared to Ksp to predict precipitation.
law of conservation of mass: The principle that mass is neither created nor destroyed in a chemical reaction.
lewis acid: A species that accepts an electron pair.
lewis base: A species that donates an electron pair.
limiting reactant: The reactant fully consumed first, determining the maximum amount of product.
limiting reagent: The reagent that runs out first and limits the amount of product formed.
molar solubility: The number of moles of a solute that dissolve per liter of saturated solution.
molar volume: The volume of one mole of a gas, 22.4 liters at standard temperature and pressure.
molarity: The number of moles of solute per liter of solution.
mole fraction: The ratio of one component's moles to the total moles in a mixture.
molecular equation: An equation showing reactants and products as complete formulas.
multi-step synthesis: Producing a target compound through a planned sequence of reactions.
nernst equation: An equation relating cell potential to standard potential and reaction quotient.
net ionic equation: An equation showing only the ions and molecules that take part in the reaction.
overall percent yield: The percent yield of a multi-step synthesis, the product of each step's yield.
oxidation: The loss of electrons by a species, increasing its oxidation state.
oxidizing acid: An acid whose anion oxidizes metals more strongly than hydrogen ion does.
oxidizing agent: The species that gains electrons and is reduced, causing oxidation of another.
percent yield: The ratio of actual to theoretical yield expressed as a percentage.
peroxide: A compound containing an oxygen-oxygen single bond, with oxygen in the -1 state.
precipitate: An insoluble solid that forms and separates from solution during a reaction.
precipitating agent: A reagent added to form a precipitate with a target ion.
qualitative analysis: A procedure identifying which ions or substances are present in a sample.
reaction quotient q: A ratio of product to reactant concentrations at any moment, compared to K to predict direction.
rechargeable battery: A cell whose reaction can be reversed by applying current to restore its charge.
reducing agent: The species that loses electrons and is oxidized, causing reduction of another.
reduction: The gain of electrons by a species, decreasing its oxidation state.
reference position of hydrogen: The standard hydrogen electrode assigned a potential of zero for comparison.
salt bridge: A connection allowing ion flow between half-cells to maintain charge balance.
saturated solution: A solution holding the maximum dissolved solute at equilibrium with undissolved solute.
selective precipitation: Separating ions by adding a reagent that precipitates one ion before another.
serial dilution: A stepwise series of dilutions producing progressively lower concentrations.
side reaction: An unwanted reaction occurring alongside the main reaction, lowering yield.
single displacement reaction: A reaction where one element replaces another in a compound.
solubility product constant, ksp: The equilibrium constant for the dissolving of a sparingly soluble ionic solid.
solubility rules: Guidelines predicting whether an ionic compound dissolves in water.
solute: The substance dissolved in a solvent to form a solution.
sparingly soluble: Describing a compound that dissolves only slightly in water.
spectator ion: An ion present but not participating in the net reaction.
spectator ions: Ions appearing unchanged on both sides of an ionic equation.
spontaneous reaction: A reaction that proceeds without continuous external energy, with negative free energy.
standard cell potential: The voltage of a cell with all species at standard conditions.
standard hydrogen electrode: The reference electrode assigned a potential of exactly zero volts.
standard reduction potential: The tendency of a half-reaction to gain electrons, measured against the hydrogen electrode.
standard solution: A solution of accurately known concentration used in titration.
standard state: The reference condition of 1 atm, 1 M, and a specified temperature for thermodynamic data.
stock solution: A concentrated solution prepared for later dilution.
stoichiometric coefficient: The number in front of a species in a balanced equation giving its mole ratio.
stoichiometric demand: The amount of a reactant required by the mole ratios of a balanced equation.
stoichiometric ratio: The mole ratio of substances given by a balanced equation.
stoichiometric workflow: The systematic sequence of conversions used to solve a stoichiometry problem.
strong acid: An acid that fully ionizes in water.
subscript: A number in a formula indicating how many atoms of an element are present.
sum rule: Adding the potentials or energies of combined half-reactions or steps appropriately.
synthesis reaction: A reaction where two or more substances combine to form a single product.
synthetic planning: Designing the sequence of reactions to make a target compound.
theoretical yield: The maximum product predicted from the limiting reactant and stoichiometry.
titrant: The solution of known concentration delivered from a burette during titration.
titration: A technique determining concentration by reacting a sample with a measured standard solution.
titration curve: A plot of pH versus volume of titrant added during a titration.
titration error: The difference between the endpoint and the true equivalence point in a titration.
volumetric flask: A flask calibrated to contain a precise volume for preparing standard solutions.
weak acid: An acid that only partially ionizes in water.
acid catalysis: Catalysis in which an acid speeds a reaction by donating protons.
activated complex: The unstable, high-energy arrangement of atoms at the peak of the reaction pathway.
activation energy: The minimum energy reactants need to reach the transition state and react.
activation energy, ea: The energy barrier that must be overcome for a reaction to proceed.
active site: The region of an enzyme where the substrate binds and reaction occurs.
adsorption: The adhesion of molecules onto a surface, a key step in heterogeneous catalysis.
alternative pathway: A different reaction route with lower activation energy, often provided by a catalyst.
alternative reaction pathway: A new mechanism with a lower energy barrier offered by a catalyst.
arrhenius equation: An equation relating rate constant to temperature and activation energy.
arrhenius plot: A graph of ln k versus 1/T whose slope gives activation energy.
average rate: The change in concentration divided by the time interval over which it occurs.
catalyst: A substance that speeds a reaction by lowering activation energy without being consumed.
catalyst effect on equilibrium: A catalyst speeds both directions equally and does not shift the equilibrium position.
catalyst selectivity: The ability of a catalyst to favor formation of one product over others.
catalytic converter: A device using catalysts to convert harmful exhaust gases into less harmful ones.
chemisorption: Adsorption involving chemical bond formation between a molecule and a surface.
collision frequency: The number of collisions between reactant particles per unit time.
collision theory: The model that reactions occur when particles collide with enough energy and proper orientation.
concentration dependent half-life: A half-life that changes with concentration, characteristic of non-first-order reactions.
concentration independent half-life: A constant half-life regardless of concentration, characteristic of first-order reactions.
consistent mechanism: A proposed mechanism whose rate law matches the experimentally observed rate law.
coordination complex: A central metal ion bonded to surrounding ligands.
desorption: The release of molecules from a surface after a surface-catalyzed reaction.
differential rate law: A rate law expressing reaction rate in terms of reactant concentrations.
effective collision: A collision with sufficient energy and correct orientation to produce a reaction.
elementary step: A single molecular event in a reaction mechanism.
energy landscape: A representation of energy changes along a reaction pathway.
enzyme: A biological catalyst, usually a protein, that speeds a specific reaction.
equilibrium constant temperature depende: The change in equilibrium constant with temperature, described by the van't Hoff equation.
equilibrium constant, k: The ratio of product to reactant activities at equilibrium for a reaction.
exponential decay: A decrease where a quantity falls by a constant fraction per unit time, as in first-order kinetics.
exponential dependence: A relationship where one quantity varies exponentially with another, as rate with temperature.
fast equilibrium approximation: Assuming a fast reversible step reaches equilibrium before the slow step in a mechanism.
first order kinetics: Kinetics where rate is proportional to the first power of one reactant's concentration.
first order signature: A constant half-life, the diagnostic feature of first-order kinetics.
frequency factor, a: The pre-exponential factor in the Arrhenius equation reflecting collision frequency and orientation.
half life: The time for the concentration of a reactant to fall to half its value.
half-life, t½: The time required for half of a reactant to be consumed.
heterogeneous catalysis: Catalysis where the catalyst is in a different phase from the reactants.
heterogeneous reaction: A reaction occurring between substances in different phases.
homogeneous catalysis: Catalysis where the catalyst is in the same phase as the reactants.
induced fit: The conformational change of an enzyme's active site as it binds a substrate.
inhibitor: A substance that slows or stops a reaction.
initial rate: The reaction rate measured at the very start before concentrations change appreciably.
initial rate method: Determining a rate law by comparing initial rates at different starting concentrations.
instantaneous rate: The reaction rate at a specific instant, the slope of the concentration-time curve.
integrated rate law: An equation relating concentration to time for a given reaction order.
kinetic accessibility: Whether a thermodynamically possible reaction proceeds fast enough to occur.
kinetic control: Conditions where the product formed fastest predominates over the most stable one.
kinetic product: The product that forms fastest, favored under kinetic control.
kinetic trapping: Trapping a system in a metastable state because the path to a stable state is too slow.
kinetically inert: Describing a species that reacts very slowly despite being thermodynamically unstable.
linear transformation: Rearranging data into a straight-line form to determine reaction order.
linearity test: Checking which plot of concentration data is linear to identify reaction order.
logarithmic shortcut: Using logarithms to simplify calculations involving exponential rate relationships.
maxwell boltzmann distribution: The distribution of molecular speeds or energies in a gas at a given temperature.
maxwell-boltzmann distribution: A curve showing how molecular energies are distributed in a sample at a temperature.
metastable state: A state stable for a time but not at the true energy minimum.
method of initial rates: Finding the rate law by measuring how initial rate changes with concentration.
molar ratio: The ratio of moles of substances in a balanced equation.
molecularity: The number of reactant particles in an elementary step.
overall order: The sum of the exponents in a reaction's rate law.
overall reaction order: The total order of a reaction, found by adding all exponents in its rate law.
pathway accessibility: Whether a reaction route is energetically and kinetically available.
potential energy diagram: A graph of energy along the reaction coordinate showing barriers and energy changes.
pseudo first order: A reaction made effectively first order by holding one reactant nearly constant.
rate constant k: The proportionality constant linking reaction rate to reactant concentrations.
rate constant temperature dependence: The increase in rate constant with temperature described by the Arrhenius equation.
rate constant, k: The temperature-dependent proportionality constant in a rate law.
rate conversion: Relating rates of appearance and disappearance using stoichiometric coefficients.
rate determining step: The slowest elementary step that controls the overall reaction rate.
rate law: An equation expressing reaction rate in terms of reactant concentrations and a rate constant.
rate law from elementary step: Deriving a rate law directly from the molecularity of an elementary step.
rate of appearance: The rate at which a product's concentration increases over time.
rate of disappearance: The rate at which a reactant's concentration decreases over time.
rate-determining step: The slowest step in a mechanism that limits the overall rate.
reaction coordinate: The progress axis of a reaction from reactants to products.
reaction intermediate: A species formed and consumed during a mechanism but not appearing in the overall equation.
reaction mechanism: The sequence of elementary steps by which a reaction occurs.
reaction order: The exponent of a reactant's concentration in the rate law.
reaction rate: The change in concentration of a reactant or product per unit time.
regeneration: The restoration of a catalyst to its original form after a reaction cycle.
residence time: The average time a molecule remains adsorbed or within a region.
reversibility under heating: The ability of a reaction or change to reverse when heat is applied.
secant line: A line through two points on a curve giving an average rate.
second order kinetics: Kinetics where rate depends on the square of one concentration or product of two.
selectivity: The preference of a reaction for forming one product over others.
sequential half-life calculation: Computing successive half-lives to track concentration over time.
shelf life: The time a substance remains usable before degrading appreciably.
slope analysis: Interpreting the slope of a linearized kinetics plot to extract a rate parameter.
slope extraction: Determining a rate constant or activation energy from a graph's slope.
steady-state approximation: Assuming an intermediate's concentration stays constant during a reaction.
substrate specificity: An enzyme's selectivity for binding only particular substrates.
successive half-life ratio: The pattern of consecutive half-lives used to identify reaction order.
tangent line: A line touching a curve at one point, giving the instantaneous rate.
temperature sensitivity: How strongly a rate constant changes with temperature, set by activation energy.
thermodynamic control: Conditions where the most stable product predominates.
thermodynamic favorability: Whether a reaction is spontaneous based on its free energy change.
thermodynamic product: The most stable product, favored under thermodynamic control.
threshold energy: The minimum energy a collision must have to react.
transition state: The highest-energy configuration along the reaction pathway.
transition state stabilization: Lowering activation energy by stabilizing the transition state, as a catalyst does.
two-point arrhenius equation: A form of the Arrhenius equation using rate constants at two temperatures to find activation energy.
unified reaction rate: A single rate expression normalized by stoichiometric coefficients for all species.
unit verification: Checking that calculated units are consistent and correct.
y intercept verification: Confirming a rate constant from the y-intercept of a linearized plot.
zero order: Kinetics where rate is independent of reactant concentration.
average bond energy: The mean energy to break a given type of bond, averaged over many molecules.
boltzmann constant, k: The constant relating average particle energy to temperature, 1.38 x 10^-23 J/K.
bomb calorimeter: A constant-volume calorimeter measuring heat of combustion.
bond dissociation energy: The energy needed to break one mole of a specific bond homolytically in the gas phase.
bond inventory: A count of bonds broken and formed used to estimate reaction enthalpy.
born-haber cycle: A thermodynamic cycle relating lattice energy to other measurable energy changes.
calorimeter constant: The heat capacity of a calorimeter, used to account for heat it absorbs.
calorimetry: The measurement of heat flow in physical and chemical processes.
coffee cup calorimeter: A simple constant-pressure calorimeter for measuring reaction heat in solution.
combustion enthalpy: The enthalpy change when one mole of a substance burns completely in oxygen.
crossover temperature: The temperature where a reaction's free energy change is zero and spontaneity reverses.
degrees of freedom: The independent ways a molecule can store energy through motion.
delta h: The enthalpy change of a process at constant pressure.
delta n gas: The change in moles of gas between products and reactants.
dissolution entropy: The entropy change accompanying a substance dissolving.
electron affinity: The energy change when a gaseous atom gains an electron.
endothermic process: A process that absorbs heat from the surroundings.
endothermic reaction: A reaction that absorbs heat, with positive enthalpy change.
enthalpy change, δh: The heat absorbed or released by a reaction at constant pressure.
enthalpy of neutralization: The heat released when an acid and base react to form water.
enthalpy of reaction: The total enthalpy change when reactants form products.
enthalpy-driven process: A process favored mainly by a negative enthalpy change.
enthalpy, h: A thermodynamic property equal to internal energy plus pressure times volume.
entropy change, δs: The change in disorder of a system during a process.
entropy of dissolution: The entropy change when a solute dissolves in a solvent.
entropy of fusion: The entropy change when a solid melts to a liquid.
entropy of surroundings: The entropy change of the surroundings, related to heat exchanged with the system.
entropy of vaporization: The entropy change when a liquid becomes a gas.
entropy-driven process: A process favored mainly by a positive entropy change.
entropy, s: A measure of the disorder or number of microstates of a system.
equilibrium constant: The ratio of product to reactant activities at equilibrium.
equilibrium temperature: The temperature at which two phases or a reaction reach equilibrium.
exothermic process: A process that releases heat to the surroundings.
exothermic reaction: A reaction that releases heat, with negative enthalpy change.
extensive property: A property depending on the amount of matter, such as mass or volume.
extrapolation: Extending a trend beyond measured data to estimate a value.
four-box model: A framework classifying spontaneity by the signs of enthalpy and entropy changes.
gas phase condition: A specification that a reaction or species is in the gaseous state.
gibbs free energy, δg: The change in free energy predicting spontaneity, ΔG = ΔH - TΔS.
heat capacity: The heat needed to raise an object's temperature by one degree.
heat capacity of calorimeter, c_cal: The heat a calorimeter absorbs per degree of temperature change.
heat loss: Heat escaping to the surroundings, a source of error in calorimetry.
heat, q: The energy transferred between objects due to a temperature difference.
hess's law: The principle that a reaction's enthalpy change is the sum of the steps' enthalpy changes.
hydration shell: The layer of water molecules surrounding a dissolved ion.
intensive property: A property independent of the amount of matter, such as temperature or density.
internal energy change, δe: The change in a system's total internal energy.
kinetic stability: Stability arising from a slow reaction rate rather than thermodynamics.
le chatelier principle: The principle that a system at equilibrium shifts to counteract an applied stress.
lewis structure: A diagram showing bonding and lone pairs of valence electrons in a molecule.
microstate: A specific arrangement of particles and energies consistent with a system's state.
natural logarithm: The logarithm to base e, used in many thermodynamic and kinetic equations.
nonstandard conditions: Conditions differing from the standard state, requiring corrections to thermodynamic values.
phase transition entropy: The entropy change accompanying a change of physical state.
phase transition temperature: The temperature at which a substance changes phase.
reaction quotient: The ratio of product to reactant concentrations at any point, compared to K.
reference point: A defined zero against which other values are measured.
residual entropy: The entropy remaining in a crystal at absolute zero due to disorder.
reversal rule: The rule that reversing a reaction changes the sign of its enthalpy or free energy.
second law of thermodynamics: The principle that the total entropy of an isolated system increases in a spontaneous process.
solvation energy: The energy released when solvent molecules surround a solute particle.
specific heat capacity: The heat needed to raise one gram of a substance by one degree.
specific heat capacity, c: The heat required per gram per degree to change a substance's temperature.
standard conditions: Reference conditions of 1 atm, 1 M, and 25 degrees Celsius for thermodynamic data.
standard enthalpy of formation: The enthalpy change forming one mole of a compound from its elements in standard states.
standard enthalpy of formation, δhf: The enthalpy change to form one mole of a compound from elements in their standard states.
standard entropy change, δs°: The entropy change of a reaction with all species at standard conditions.
standard free energy change: The Gibbs free energy change with all species at standard conditions.
standard free energy of formation: The free energy change forming one mole of a compound from elements in standard states.
standard molar entropy, s°: The absolute entropy of one mole of a substance at standard conditions.
state function: A property depending only on the state of a system, not the path taken.
statistical thermodynamics: The study of thermodynamic properties from the statistics of particle microstates.
stoichiometric scaling: Adjusting a reaction's enthalpy proportionally when its coefficients are scaled.
sublimation enthalpy: The enthalpy change converting a solid directly to a gas.
surroundings: Everything outside the system that can exchange energy or matter with it.
system: The part of the universe under study in a thermodynamic analysis.
system only criterion: Using only the system's free energy to judge spontaneity at constant T and P.
systematic error: A consistent error biasing measurements in one direction.
temperature change, δt: The difference between final and initial temperatures.
temperature dependence: How a quantity varies with temperature.
temperature-dependent spontaneity: Spontaneity that changes with temperature when enthalpy and entropy oppose each other.
temperature-independent spontaneity: Spontaneity that holds at all temperatures when enthalpy and entropy agree.
thermochemical equation: A balanced equation including its enthalpy change.
thermodynamic driving force: The free energy change pushing a reaction toward products.
thermodynamic stability: Stability based on having lower free energy than alternatives.
third law of thermodynamics: The principle that the entropy of a perfect crystal is zero at absolute zero.
trouton's rule: The approximation that many liquids have a similar entropy of vaporization near 85 J/mol K.
unit conversion: Changing a quantity from one unit to another using conversion factors.
δg versus t graph: A plot of free energy change against temperature showing where spontaneity changes.
activity: The effective concentration of a species in thermodynamic expressions.
approach to equilibrium: The progression of a reaction toward its equilibrium state.
approximation failure: The breakdown of a simplifying assumption when its conditions are not met.
approximation method: Using a simplifying assumption to make an equilibrium calculation tractable.
approximation validity: Whether a simplifying assumption is justified, often by the five percent rule.
back substitution: Inserting an approximate answer back into an equation to check or refine it.
complex ion: A central metal ion bonded to surrounding ligands forming a charged species.
complexation equilibrium: The equilibrium between a metal ion, ligands, and the complex ion they form.
compression shift: The shift in a gaseous equilibrium when volume is decreased, favoring fewer moles of gas.
concentration change: An alteration in concentration that shifts an equilibrium position.
concentration constraint: A limitation set by available concentrations in an equilibrium problem.
concentration stress: A change in concentration that disturbs an equilibrium per Le Chatelier's principle.
conjugate base of strong acid: The very weak, non-basic anion left after a strong acid donates its proton.
conjugate base of weak acid: The base formed when a weak acid loses a proton, capable of hydrolysis.
coupled equilibria: Two or more equilibria that share a common species and influence one another.
coupling point: The shared species or step linking two coupled equilibria.
cube root relationship: A solubility relationship where ion concentration depends on the cube root of Ksp.
delta n: The change in moles of gas between products and reactants.
dilution effect: The shift in equilibrium or pH caused by adding solvent.
direction of spontaneous change: The direction a reaction moves to reach equilibrium, set by comparing Q and K.
discriminant: The expression under the square root in the quadratic formula determining the roots.
dissociation constant, kd: The equilibrium constant for a complex or molecule breaking into its components.
dynamic equilibrium: A state where forward and reverse reactions occur at equal rates with constant concentrations.
effective equilibrium constant: An overall constant combining several equilibria into one.
enthalpy contribution: The portion of free energy change arising from enthalpy.
entropy contribution: The portion of free energy change arising from entropy times temperature.
equilibrium constant k: The ratio of product to reactant activities at equilibrium.
equilibrium constant kc: The equilibrium constant expressed using molar concentrations.
equilibrium shift: A change in the equilibrium position in response to a stress.
extent of reaction: How far a reaction proceeds toward products at equilibrium.
five percent rule: The guideline that an approximation is valid if the change is under five percent of the initial value.
formation constant, kf: The equilibrium constant for forming a complex ion from a metal ion and ligands.
forward rate: The rate of the reaction proceeding from reactants to products.
forward shift: A shift of equilibrium toward the products.
heterogeneous equilibrium: An equilibrium involving species in more than one phase.
higher order equilibrium expression: An equilibrium expression leading to a polynomial higher than quadratic.
homogeneous equilibrium: An equilibrium with all species in the same phase.
inert gas: A nonreacting gas whose addition at constant volume does not shift equilibrium.
kelvin temperature: The absolute temperature scale used in thermodynamic calculations.
large k value: A large equilibrium constant indicating a product-favored reaction.
law of mass action: The principle defining the equilibrium constant as a ratio of product to reactant activities.
le chatelier's principle: The principle that an equilibrium shifts to oppose an applied change.
ligand: An ion or molecule donating a lone pair to bond with a central metal ion.
limiting scenario: An extreme case used to bound the behavior of an equilibrium system.
magnitude relationship: A comparison of the relative sizes of equilibrium constants or concentrations.
molar solubility, s: The moles of a solute dissolving per liter of saturated solution.
mole ratio comparison: Comparing mole ratios to identify limiting amounts or reaction direction.
natural logarithm relationship: The link between free energy and the equilibrium constant through ln K.
overall equilibrium constant: The product of the constants of sequential equilibria combined into one.
ph-dependent solubility: The variation of a salt's solubility with the pH of the solution.
phase identification: Determining the physical states of species in an equilibrium.
physical validity: Whether a calculated result is physically reasonable, such as a positive concentration.
product-favored reaction: A reaction with a large equilibrium constant favoring products at equilibrium.
protonation of anions: The gaining of protons by basic anions, affecting pH and solubility.
pure liquid: A pure liquid whose activity is one and is excluded from equilibrium expressions.
pure solid: A pure solid whose activity is one and is excluded from equilibrium expressions.
pure substance concentration: The constant, omitted activity of a pure solid or liquid in equilibrium expressions.
q greater than k: The condition where the reaction quotient exceeds K, so the reaction shifts toward reactants.
q less than k: The condition where the reaction quotient is below K, so the reaction shifts toward products.
reactant-favored reaction: A reaction with a small equilibrium constant favoring reactants at equilibrium.
reaction direction: The way a reaction proceeds to reach equilibrium, found by comparing Q and K.
reaction free energy change, δg: The free energy change of a reaction at given conditions, indicating spontaneity.
reaction quotient, q: The ratio of product to reactant activities at any moment, compared to K.
reverse rate: The rate of the reaction proceeding from products back to reactants.
reverse reaction setup: Arranging an equilibrium problem for the reverse direction, inverting K.
reverse shift: A shift of equilibrium toward the reactants.
reversible reaction: A reaction that can proceed in both forward and reverse directions to reach equilibrium.
sequential equilibria: Multiple equilibria occurring in steps, where each product feeds the next.
small k value: A small equilibrium constant indicating a reactant-favored reaction.
small x approximation: Assuming the change x is negligible compared to initial concentration to simplify equilibrium math.
spontaneity: Whether a process occurs on its own, determined by the sign of free energy change.
standard free energy change, δg°: The free energy change with all species at standard conditions.
standard quadratic form: The form ax^2 + bx + c = 0 solved with the quadratic formula in equilibrium problems.
stress: A disturbance such as concentration, pressure, or temperature change applied to an equilibrium.
supersaturated solution: An unstable solution holding more solute than its equilibrium solubility.
temperature dependence of k: The change in equilibrium constant with temperature, depending on reaction enthalpy.
temperature stress: A temperature change that shifts equilibrium, treating heat as a reactant or product.
threshold concentration: The concentration at which precipitation or a change begins.
unsaturated solution: A solution holding less solute than its maximum, able to dissolve more.
van't hoff equation: An equation relating the change in equilibrium constant to temperature and reaction enthalpy.
acetate ion: The conjugate base of acetic acid, CH3COO-.
acid dissociation constant ka: The equilibrium constant for an acid donating a proton in water.
acid dissociation constant, ka: The equilibrium constant measuring the strength of a weak acid.
acid-base indicator: A weak acid or base that changes color with pH.
additive color absorption: The combining of absorbed wavelengths determining a solution's observed color.
adduct: A product formed by the direct combination of two molecules, as in a Lewis acid-base reaction.
adduct formation: The joining of a Lewis acid and base to form a single adduct.
alpha carbon: The carbon atom adjacent to a functional group such as a carbonyl.
amphiprotic species: A species that can both donate and accept a proton.
amphoteric: Able to react as either an acid or a base.
amphoteric species: A substance that can act as both an acid and a base depending on conditions.
autoionization: The self-ionization of a substance, as water forming H+ and OH-.
autoionization of water: The reaction where water molecules transfer protons to form H3O+ and OH-.
averaging formula: A formula used to find the pH at a point where two species' values are averaged.
base dissociation constant, kb: The equilibrium constant measuring the strength of a weak base.
base hydrolysis: The reaction of a base with water producing hydroxide ions.
buffer mechanism: How a buffer's conjugate pair neutralizes added acid or base to resist pH change.
buffer range: The pH range, about pKa plus or minus one, where a buffer works effectively.
buffer solution: A solution of a weak acid and its conjugate base that resists pH change.
buffer system selection: Choosing a buffer whose pKa is near the desired pH.
buffering capacity: The quantity of acid or base a buffer can absorb before its pH shifts significantly.
capacity depletion: The exhaustion of a buffer's ability to resist pH change.
central atom electronegativity: The electronegativity of an oxyacid's central atom, affecting its acid strength.
charge delocalization: The spreading of charge over several atoms, stabilizing a conjugate base.
competing equilibria: Two or more equilibria simultaneously affecting the same species.
complete dissociation: The full separation of a strong electrolyte into ions in water.
conjugate acid: The species formed when a base gains a proton.
conjugate base: The species formed when an acid loses a proton.
conjugate base stability: The stability of the anion formed when an acid loses a proton, which raises acid strength.
conjugated system: An arrangement of alternating bonds allowing electron delocalization.
coordinate covalent bond: A covalent bond where both shared electrons come from one atom.
crossover point: The point where two competing species or curves are equal.
direct mixing: Preparing a buffer or solution by directly combining its components.
dominant ionization step: The ionization step contributing most to the pH of a polyprotic acid.
early-firing indicator: An indicator that changes color before the equivalence point, with too low a pKa.
electron withdrawal: The pulling of electron density away by electronegative groups, stabilizing a conjugate base.
electron withdrawing group: A substituent that pulls electron density away, increasing acid strength.
electron-deficient species: A species with an incomplete octet or empty orbital that acts as a Lewis acid.
empty orbital: A vacant orbital that can accept an electron pair, enabling Lewis acidity.
endpoint precision: The accuracy with which a titration endpoint matches the equivalence point.
equilibrium concentration: The concentration of a species when a reaction reaches equilibrium.
hydrogen carbonate ion, hco₃⁻: The amphiprotic bicarbonate ion that can donate or accept a proton.
hydrogen ion concentration: The concentration of H+ ions in solution, determining acidity.
hydrohalic acids: The binary acids of the halogens, such as HCl and HBr.
hydrolysis of conjugate acid: The reaction of a conjugate acid with water, lowering pH.
hydrolysis of conjugate base: The reaction of a conjugate base with water, raising pH.
in situ formation: The production of a needed species within the reaction mixture itself.
indicator pka: The pKa of an indicator, near which it changes color.
inductive effect: The transmission of charge through bonds by electronegative groups, affecting acidity.
inflection point: The steep midpoint of a titration curve marking the equivalence point.
initial ph: The pH of a solution before any titrant is added.
ion product constant for water, kw: The equilibrium constant for water autoionization, 1.0 x 10^-14 at 25 degrees Celsius.
isoelectric point: The pH at which a molecule carries no net electrical charge.
ka times kb equals kw: The relationship that a conjugate acid-base pair's Ka and Kb multiply to give Kw.
late-firing indicator: An indicator that changes color after the equivalence point, with too high a pKa.
logarithmic ratio: A ratio expressed on a logarithmic scale, as in the Henderson-Hasselbalch equation.
logarithmic scale: A scale based on powers of ten, such as the pH scale.
maximum buffering capacity: The greatest buffering ability, reached when conjugate acid and base are equal.
metal ion hydrolysis: The reaction of a hydrated metal ion with water, producing an acidic solution.
monoprotic acid: An acid that donates only one proton per molecule.
negligible contribution: A small effect ignored in a calculation, such as water's H+ in a strong acid solution.
neutral solution: A solution with equal H+ and OH-, having a pH of 7 at 25 degrees Celsius.
orbital overlap: The merging of atomic orbitals that forms a covalent bond.
percent dissociation: The fraction of an electrolyte that dissociates, expressed as a percentage.
percent ionization: The percentage of a weak acid or base molecules that ionize in solution.
perchloric acid: HClO4, one of the strongest common oxyacids, a strong acid.
ph gradient: A continuous range of pH values that a solution passes through rather than a single sharp transition point.
polyprotic acid: An acid that can donate more than one proton, releasing each in a separate equilibrium step with its own Ka.
